title: 3 Standard Stoppages, Marcel Duchamp’s MoMA set
dateKind: The museum’s date and place of making for the assembled work
about: The box brings together three threads, canvas and glass supports, and three wooden templates. MoMA relates Duchamp’s account of dropping a metre of thread and fixing each of the three resulting curves.
limit: The traces fix three outcomes. A starting length and a gap between ends describe different things even when both are measured in the same unit.
line: Pull the thread out and the last point looks inevitable. Put it down slack and the ruler would still find the same length in your hand. Keep both marks where the next visitor can reach them.
job: The scale keeper can use a gap. The drawing table wants a way to keep a chance shape after the thread is lifted.
near: The scale keeper fixes the gap label beside the practice board. Now the maker can use the marked ends without calling that gap the length of the thread.
study: A visitor traces the practice curve onto a fresh leaf, then stretches the same thread over the ruler. The leaf preserves this fall of the thread for another reader.

revisit.method: See where a familiar straight rule leaves the thread behind.
revisit.hint: Bring the Stoppages to the long ruler below the Hall of Firsts.

title: The London School of Economics MONIAC, Science Museum Group 1995-210
date: 1949 · this teaching machine ran at LSE until May 1992
dateKind: The catalogue’s making date and the separately documented end of its teaching use
about: Bill Phillips devised this hydraulic economic computer. White Ellerton Limited made it in London in 1949. The Science Museum Group traces this machine to the London School of Economics, where it ran until May 1992.
limit: The demonstration keeps a split fixed so an observer can see the effect of changing intake. An actual economy can change the split as well as the intake.
line: Stand where the reservoirs show. Send three units, then six, with the same share reserved in each run. It helps people follow the money before they argue about what anyone would really save.
job: One market reader needs to see when spending arrives. A second wants the reserve rule attached before passing on the forecast.
near: The scale keeper follows the arriving units rather than the level already held in reserve. The model slips now show which run moved money sooner.
study: The study table writes the reserve rule beside the forecast. A later reader can change the rule and compare a new result with the fixed rule used here.

revisit.method: Open the receipts drawer that separates a stock from a flow.
revisit.hint: Bring the MONIAC to the two-slot drawer beside the south reading lane.

title: Theseus, the magnetic mouse and maze in the MIT Museum
dateKind: Year the machine was created and the separate year the museum received it
about: The MIT Museum keeps the mouse, its configurable table-top maze and related parts and working records. MIT describes a magnetically moved mouse controlled by a relay circuit beneath the maze.
limit: A shorter second run in the practice maze shows what a saved route can do here. It leaves open what this kind of machine could know about a new maze.
line: You can look at the mouse all afternoon and never see its route. Lift the floor and watch which direction the relay record sends it. Keep the boards in the same places for your second run.
job: A visitor sees that the mouse arrives sooner. A keeper wants people to be able to follow which part of the machine kept the route.
near: The keeper posts the saved path on the public bench. Visitors can lap the same maze again and read the number of moves beside each run.
study: The study reader moves the record to the slot below the board. The same mouse runs over it again, so the next visitor can compare where the route lives.

revisit.method: Find the route record under the archive’s old practice maze.
revisit.hint: Bring Theseus to the low maze near the south reading lane.
